type: direction; also particle — the second word of many phrasal verbs (*give up*, *eat up*)
position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but always after a pronoun (*pick it up*)
modifies: verbs, especially verbs of motion; phrasal verbs
contrast: With an object after it, *up* is a preposition (*walk up the hill*); with none, it is the adverb (*look up*). As a particle it can come before or after a noun object (*pick up the box*, *pick the box up*) but must follow a pronoun: *pick it up*, never *pick up it*. Very often *up* does not mean вверх at all but ‘completely’, like a Russian perfective prefix: *eat up* = съесть, *use up* = израсходовать, *drink up* = допить. *What's up?* and *Time's up* are adjective uses.

senses.gloss: Toward a higher place or position.
examples: She looked *up* at the sky.
Pick your clothes *up* off the floor.
Is this elevator going *up*?

senses.gloss: Into an upright position, standing or sitting straight.
examples: Please stand *up* when the judge comes in.
Sit *up* straight at the table.
He helped the old man *up* after he slipped.

senses.gloss: Out of bed; awake.
examples: Are the kids *up* yet?
We stayed *up* until two watching the game.
I got *up* at six this morning.

senses.gloss: To a higher amount, level, volume, or intensity.
examples: Gas prices went *up* again this week.
Can you turn the volume *up*?
Speak *up*, please; I can't hear you.

senses.gloss: Completely, so that nothing is left or the action is finished.
examples: Eat *up* your vegetables.
Somebody used *up* all the hot water.
Clean *up* your room before dinner.

senses.gloss: So as to be closed, fastened, or tied together.
examples: Zip *up* your jacket; it's freezing.
Don't forget to lock *up* when you leave.
Tie *up* the garbage bag before you take it out.

senses.gloss: Into pieces or small parts.
examples: She tore the letter *up* and threw it away.
Cut the chicken *up* into small pieces.

senses.gloss: Into existence, view, or attention.
examples: Your name came *up* at the meeting.
Sorry, something came *up* and I can't make it.
He didn't show *up* until nine.

senses.gloss: Close to a person or place, approaching.
examples: A stranger came *up* and asked for directions.
A black car pulled *up* outside the house.
Go ahead, I'll catch *up*.

senses.gloss: To or in the north, or to a place thought of as more important or central.
senses.ru: на север; в город, в центр
examples: We're driving *up* to Maine for the weekend.
They moved *up* north after they retired.

senses.gloss: Ahead of an opponent by a stated score.
examples: We were ten points *up* at halftime.
The Yankees were two runs *up* going into the ninth.

type: direction; also particle — the second word of many phrasal verbs (*calm down*, *break down*)
position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but always after a pronoun (*write it down*)
modifies: verbs, especially verbs of motion; phrasal verbs
contrast: *down the street* is the preposition and means ‘along, по улице’, not ‘downhill’. The pronoun goes before the particle: *write it down*, never *write down it*. *I feel down* (мне грустно) is an adjective. *Down to Texas* and *up to Chicago* for south and north are everyday American speech, even across flat land.

senses.gloss: Toward a lower place or position.
examples: Sit *down* and make yourself at home.
She looked *down* at her shoes.
The sun goes *down* around eight in the summer.

senses.gloss: To a lower amount, level, volume, speed, or intensity.
examples: Turn the music *down*; the baby's asleep.
Prices have finally come *down*.
Slow *down*, you're driving too fast.

senses.gloss: So as to stop working or operating.
examples: My car broke *down* on the highway.
The factory shut *down* last year.
The website went *down* for an hour this morning.

senses.gloss: On paper; in writing.
examples: Write the address *down* before you forget it.
Did you get all of that *down*?

senses.gloss: Firmly in place, or so as to be found or caught.
examples: Tie the tarp *down* so it doesn't blow away.
Nail the boards *down* before the storm hits.
The police finally tracked him *down*.

senses.gloss: To or in the south, or away from the center of things.
examples: We drove *down* to Florida for spring break.
My grandparents live *down* south.

senses.gloss: From an earlier generation or time to a later one.
examples: The ring was handed *down* from my grandmother.
These stories have been passed *down* for centuries.

senses.gloss: As a first payment, with the rest paid later.
examples: We put ten percent *down* on the house.
Drive it home today with no money *down*.

senses.gloss: Behind an opponent by a stated score.
examples: We were *down* by six at halftime.
They came back from three goals *down*.

type: direction; also place and particle (*fill in*, *give in*)
position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but after a pronoun (*hand it in*)
modifies: verbs, especially verbs of motion; phrasal verbs
contrast: Russian *в* covers three English forms: *come in* (adverb, no object), *come into the room* (preposition *into*, movement) and *be in the room* (preposition *in*, location). *Come in the house* is common in American speech, but *into* is the standard for movement. *in* meaning ‘fashionable’ (*Wide jeans are in*) is an adjective.

senses.gloss: Into or toward the inside of a place, container, or vehicle.
examples: Come *in* and sit down.
Get *in*, I'll give you a ride.
The roof caved *in* under the snow.

senses.gloss: At home or at one's place of work.
examples: Is Dr. Patel *in* today?
I'm not coming *in* tomorrow; I'm sick.
We stayed *in* and watched a movie.

senses.gloss: Arriving, or received at the place where it is expected.
examples: What time does your flight get *in*?
The election results are starting to come *in*.

senses.gloss: To a person or organization in authority, handed over.
examples: Please hand your essays *in* by Friday.
Viewers sent *in* thousands of photos.

senses.gloss: Taking part, included with others.
examples: If you're ordering pizza, count me *in*.
Everyone joined *in* on the chorus.

senses.gloss: Into a space, so as to fill or complete it.
examples: Fill *in* the blanks with the correct word.
The kids colored *in* the pictures.

type: direction; also place and particle (*find out*, *run out*)
position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but after a pronoun (*take it out*)
modifies: verbs, especially verbs of motion; phrasal verbs
contrast: Before a place, standard English uses *out of*: *get out of the car*. American English drops *of* before *door* and *window* (*look out the window*, *run out the door*), where British keeps it. The pictures can run opposite ways: *the lights went out* = погасли, but *the stars came out* = появились. *out* in baseball (*he's out*) is an adjective.

senses.gloss: Away from the inside of a place or container.
examples: The kids ran *out* into the yard.
Can you take the trash *out*?
Get *out*!

senses.gloss: Away from home or work, often for a social activity.
examples: Sorry, she's *out* for lunch.
Let's eat *out* tonight.
We went *out* on Friday night.

senses.gloss: So as to be found, understood, or solved.
examples: Did you ever find *out* who sent the flowers?
I can't figure *out* this remote.
Don't worry, we'll work it *out*.

senses.gloss: So as to stop burning or shining.
examples: The lights went *out* during the storm.
Put your cigarette *out*, please.

senses.gloss: Until finished, or until nothing is left.
examples: Our money ran *out* in the second week.
Hear me *out* before you decide.
The concert sold *out* in ten minutes.

senses.gloss: Aloud, so as to be clearly heard.
examples: Read the list *out* loud.
She cried *out* in pain.

senses.gloss: Into view, or into public knowledge or sale.
examples: The sun came *out* after lunch.
Her new album comes *out* next month.
Sooner or later, the truth will come *out*.

senses.gloss: So as to be removed or left out.
examples: Cross *out* the wrong answer.
Leave the onions *out*, please.

senses.gloss: To many people, distributed.
examples: The teacher handed *out* the tests.
They're giving *out* free samples at the store.

senses.gloss: Into unconsciousness.
examples: He passed *out* from the heat.
The boxer was knocked *out* in the third round.

senses.gloss: Far away from land, a town, or the center.
examples: They live way *out* in the country.
The boat was a mile *out* when the storm hit.

type: direction; also time (*back in 2010*) and particle (*pay back*, *hold back*)
position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but after a pronoun (*give it back*)
modifies: verbs; phrasal verbs; time phrases (*back in the day*)
contrast: *back* is not ‘again’: *come back* = вернуться, *come again* = прийти ещё раз. With a pronoun: *give it back*, never *give back it*. *a few years back* is informal American for *ago*. *Push a meeting back* makes it later; *move it forward* usually means earlier — say the date if it matters.

senses.gloss: To the place, person, or condition where someone or something was before.
examples: I'll be *back* in five minutes.
Put the milk *back* in the fridge.
She went *back* to sleep.

senses.gloss: In return or in reply.
examples: Can I call you *back* in an hour?
He never paid me *back*.
She smiled *back* at him.

senses.gloss: Toward the rear, away from the front.
examples: Step *back* from the edge.
Lean *back* and relax.
Don't look *back*.

senses.gloss: In or into the past; ago.
examples: *Back* in the 1990s, few people had a cell phone.
I met her a few years *back*.

senses.gloss: Under control, kept from moving forward or coming out.
examples: The police held the crowd *back*.
She fought *back* tears.

senses.gloss: To a later time, or to an earlier setting on a clock.
examples: The meeting was pushed *back* to Friday.
Remember to set your clocks *back* on Sunday.

type: direction; also time and particle (*come forward*, *put forward*)
position: end — after the verb or its object
comparison: not gradable — *further forward* does the comparing
contrast: American English says *forward*; British also *forwards*. *Move the meeting forward* usually means earlier, but some Americans hear later — name the day. *look forward to* takes a noun or *-ing*: *I look forward to seeing you*, never *to see you*. *forward* is also a verb (*forward an email*).

senses.gloss: Toward the front, or in the direction one is facing.
examples: Take one step *forward*.
She leaned *forward* to hear better.
The car jerked *forward* and stalled.

senses.gloss: Toward the future or toward progress.
examples: It's time to move *forward* with the plan.
From this day *forward*, things will be different.

senses.gloss: Into view or public attention, so as to be offered or known.
examples: Two witnesses have come *forward*.
She put *forward* a new proposal.

senses.gloss: To an earlier date, or to a later setting on a clock.
examples: Set your clocks *forward* one hour tonight.
We moved the deadline *forward* to Monday.

position: end — after the verb or its object
form: -ward from *back*; American English uses *backward* and *backwards* alike
contrast: Both *backward* and *backwards* are American; the adjective is only *backward* (*a backward glance*; *a backward country* = отсталая). Three Russian phrases, three English ones: задом наперёд = *backward* (*your shirt is on backward*), наизнанку = *inside out*, вверх ногами = *upside down*.

senses.gloss: Toward the back, or in the direction behind one.
examples: He took a step *backward*.
She fell *backward* into the pool.

senses.gloss: In reverse order, from the end to the beginning.
examples: Can you say the alphabet *backward*?
Count *backward* from ten.

senses.gloss: With the back part in front.
examples: You have your shirt on *backward*.
He wears his baseball cap *backward*.

senses.gloss: Toward the past, or to a worse state.
examples: Critics say the new law takes the country *backward*.
Critics called the decision a big step *backward*.

senses.gloss: Thoroughly, in every detail (in *backward and forward*).
examples: She knows the rules *backward* and forward.
I've read that contract *backward* and forward.

position: end; *upward of* goes before a number
contrast: American English prefers *upward*, British *upwards*, though Americans often say *upwards of* too. *upward of 50* means ‘more than 50’ (свыше), not ‘up to 50’. The adjective goes before a noun: *an upward trend*.

senses.gloss: Toward a higher place.
examples: The balloon floated *upward* into the clouds.
Point the camera *upward*.

senses.gloss: Toward a higher amount, level, or rank.
examples: Home prices are moving *upward* again.
The forecast was revised *upward*.

senses.gloss: More than a stated number (in *upward of*).
examples: *Upward of* 500 people showed up.
The repairs could cost *upward of* $10,000.

position: end — after the verb, or after *from* + a rank (*from the CEO downward*)
contrast: American *downward*, British *downwards*. The adjective sits before a noun (*a downward spiral*). For лицом вниз the everyday phrase is *face down*, not *face downward*.

senses.gloss: Toward a lower place.
examples: The path slopes *downward* to the beach.
She glanced *downward* at her phone.

senses.gloss: Toward a lower amount or level.
examples: Sales estimates were revised *downward*.
Interest rates are heading *downward*.

senses.gloss: From a higher rank or level to all the lower ones.
examples: Everyone from the CEO *downward* took a pay cut.
The rule applies to all staff, from managers *downward*.

position: end — after the verb
contrast: Don't confuse with *inwardly*, which means ‘privately, in one's mind’: *Inwardly, she was furious* = в душе. The adjective goes before a noun: *inward calm*. American *inward*, British also *inwards*.

senses.gloss: Toward the inside or the center.
examples: The door opens *inward*.
The walls began to bend *inward*.

senses.gloss: Toward one's own mind and feelings.
examples: After the loss, he turned *inward* and stopped calling friends.
Meditation asks you to look *inward*.

position: end — after the verb
contrast: For внешне use *outwardly*: *He was outwardly calm*, never *He was outward calm*. The adjective goes before a noun: *outward appearance*. American *outward*, British also *outwards*.

senses.gloss: Toward the outside, or away from the center.
examples: The door opens *outward*.
The city keeps spreading *outward*.

senses.gloss: Toward other people or the world outside oneself or one's group.
examples: The company needs to look *outward* for new ideas.
Try to focus *outward* instead of worrying about yourself.

position: end — after the verb
contrast: In everyday American speech the plain compass word is the adverb: *drive north*, *head north*, *up north*. *northward* sounds written or technical. No *to* before the bare word: *go north*, but *to the north*.

senses.gloss: Toward the north.
examples: The storm is moving *northward* along the coast.
Many birds fly *northward* in the spring.
The highway runs *northward* to the Canadian border.

position: end — after the verb
contrast: Everyday American speech says *go south*, *head south*, *down south*; *southward* belongs to writing and weather reports. No *to* before the bare word: *go south*, but *to the south*.

senses.gloss: Toward the south.
examples: The river flows *southward* to the Gulf of Mexico.
Every fall, the geese head *southward*.
The hurricane turned *southward* overnight.

position: end — after the verb
contrast: In speech Americans say *drive east*, *head east*; *eastward* sounds written. *back East* in American speech means ‘in the eastern United States’. No *to* before the bare word: *go east*, but *to the east*.

senses.gloss: Toward the east.
examples: The storm system is moving *eastward* across the plains.
They sailed *eastward* toward Europe.
The city has grown *eastward* over the years.

position: end — after the verb
contrast: In speech Americans say *drive west*, *head west*; *westward* is written and historical (*westward expansion*, the 19th-century settlement of the American West, uses the adjective). No *to* before the bare word: *go west*, but *to the west*.

senses.gloss: Toward the west.
examples: Settlers pushed *westward* in the 1800s.
The flight headed *westward* over the Pacific.
The wildfire spread *westward* overnight.

position: end — after the verb
contrast: The everyday adverb is *home* with no *to*: *go home*, *head home*. *homeward* is literary; *homeward bound* (на пути домой) is a fixed phrase.

senses.gloss: Toward home.
examples: We finally started *homeward* after midnight.
The birds flew *homeward* as the sun set.
At last the soldiers turned *homeward*.

position: end — after the verb or its object
contrast: Always with *-s*; there is no adverb *sideway*. In informal American English *go sideways* means ‘go wrong’, not a literal direction. A *sideways move* at work is neither a promotion nor a demotion.

senses.gloss: To or toward one side.
examples: The crab scuttled *sideways* across the sand.
She stepped *sideways* to let him pass.
The car skidded *sideways* on the ice.

senses.gloss: With one side facing forward or up.
examples: Turn the couch *sideways* to get it through the door.
He sat *sideways* in the chair.

senses.gloss: To a job or position of about the same rank.
examples: She moved *sideways* into marketing.
He didn't get promoted; he was shifted *sideways*.

senses.gloss: Informally, into a bad or unexpected state; wrong.
examples: The deal went *sideways* at the last minute.
Things went *sideways* when the power went out.

position: end — after the verb or its object
contrast: The opposite is American *counterclockwise*, British *anticlockwise*. The same form is an adjective before a noun: *a clockwise direction*.

senses.gloss: In the direction the hands of a clock move.
examples: Turn the lid *clockwise* to close it.
The numbers on the dial go *clockwise* from zero to ten.
Stir the sauce *clockwise* for two minutes.

position: end — after the verb or its object
contrast: American *counterclockwise* is British *anticlockwise*; Americans understand the British word but don't use it. The same form is an adjective: *a counterclockwise turn*.

senses.gloss: In the direction opposite to the way the hands of a clock move.
examples: Turn the knob *counterclockwise* to open the valve.
The skaters moved *counterclockwise* around the rink.
Loosen the bolt by turning it *counterclockwise*.

position: end — right after the verb (*turn left*)
contrast: No preposition after *turn*: *turn left*, never *turn to left*; with the noun it is *turn to the left* or American *take a left*. Don't confuse it with *left*, the past tense of *leave* (*She left early*). *right* works the same way and is in the flat-adverb group.

senses.gloss: Toward or on the left side.
examples: Turn *left* at the light.
Look *left*, then right, before you cross.
Scoot *left* a little so I can sit down.

senses.gloss: Toward liberal or left-wing political views.
examples: The party has moved *left* on climate policy.
Voters in the city lean *left*.

type: direction; also particle (*get along*, *go along with*)
position: end — after the verb or its object
contrast: With an object *along* is a preposition meaning вдоль (*walk along the river*); without one it is the adverb (*walk along*). *along with* means ‘together with’. *get along* = ладить; British also *get on*. *all along* means ‘the whole time’, not ‘all the way along something’.

senses.gloss: Forward, onward, on one's way.
examples: A police officer told the crowd to move *along*.
We were driving *along* when a tire blew.

senses.gloss: With oneself or with someone else.
examples: Bring your sister *along*.
Can I come *along*?
Take an umbrella *along* just in case.

senses.gloss: Making progress toward completion.
examples: How's your essay coming *along*?
The new house is coming *along* nicely.

senses.gloss: The whole time, from the beginning (in *all along*).
examples: I knew *all along* that he was lying.
The keys were in my pocket *all along*.

senses.gloss: In agreement or on good terms with others.
examples: I didn't agree, but I went *along* with it.
My sister and I get *along* great.
Just play *along* for now.

position: end — after the verb or after a measurement (*a mile across*)
contrast: Russian через splits in two: *across* is over a surface or a line (*across the street*, *across the bridge*); *through* is inside something (*through the forest*, *through the tunnel*). Both of those are prepositions; the adverb has no object (*swim across*). *across from* is American for напротив. *acrost* is nonstandard.

senses.gloss: From one side to the other.
examples: The river was too wide to swim *across*.
Wait for the light before you walk *across*.

senses.gloss: Measured from one side to the other.
examples: The crater is about a mile *across*.
Order the pizza that's sixteen inches *across*.

senses.gloss: So as to be understood.
examples: She had trouble getting her point *across*.
The ad gets the message *across* in ten seconds.

senses.gloss: Giving a particular impression (in *come across*).
examples: He comes *across* as shy, but he isn't.
Did I come *across* as rude?

senses.gloss: In a crossword, reading from left to right.
examples: What's the answer to 12 *across*?
I got 4 *across* but not 7 down.

type: direction; also place, degree (*around 50*) and particle
position: end; before a number when it means ‘about’
contrast: American English uses *around* where British often says *round* (*turn around*, *go around*) or *about* (*around 50 people*, *walk around*). Meaning ‘about’, it goes before the number: *around six*, never *six around*. With an object it is a preposition: *around the corner*.

senses.gloss: From place to place, here and there.
examples: We walked *around* downtown for an hour.
Mind if I look *around*?
She travels *around* a lot for work.

senses.gloss: So as to face the opposite direction.
examples: Turn *around* and look at me.
He spun *around* when he heard his name.

senses.gloss: Approximately.
examples: *Around* 200 people came to the wedding.
The tickets cost *around* forty dollars.

senses.gloss: Nearby; present and available.
examples: Is Mike *around*?
There was nobody *around* to help.

senses.gloss: In a circle, or turning about a center.
examples: The fan turned slowly *around*.
The kids spun *around* until they got dizzy.

senses.gloss: On every side; surrounding.
examples: The cabin has mountains all *around*.
A crowd gathered *around* to watch.

senses.gloss: In the reverse way (in *the other way around*).
examples: I don't owe you money; it's the other way *around*.
I thought the dog was chasing the cat, but it was the other way *around*.

senses.gloss: In existence or in use.
examples: Vinyl records have been *around* for over a century.
Smartphones weren't *around* when I was a kid.

senses.gloss: Without a purpose, doing nothing useful.
examples: We just sat *around* all afternoon.
Stop fooling *around* and do your homework.

senses.gloss: By a longer route, not directly.
examples: The bridge was closed, so we had to go *around*.
We took the long way *around*.

senses.gloss: So that each person gets a share.
examples: Is there enough cake to go *around*?
They passed the photos *around*.

senses.gloss: To a new opinion, especially one first rejected (in *come around*).
examples: She hated the idea at first, but she came *around*.
Give him time; he'll come *around*.

senses.gloss: In circumference, measured all the way around.
examples: The trunk of the old oak is nearly ten feet *around*.
How big *around* is your wrist?

type: direction; also frequency (*start over*) and particle
position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but after a pronoun (*think it over*)
modifies: verbs; phrasal verbs; numbers (*65 and over*)
contrast: American *start over* and *do it over* mean ‘again, заново’ — British says *start again*. *The game is over* (закончилась) is an adjective. With an object *over* is a preposition (*over the bridge*). *come over* means ‘come to visit’, not перейти.

senses.gloss: Across or above something, from one side to the other.
examples: A helicopter flew *over* at dawn.
The fence was too high to climb *over*.

senses.gloss: To or at a place, especially someone's home, or across a short distance.
examples: Come *over* for dinner on Saturday.
We had some friends *over* last night.
Bring that chair *over* here.

senses.gloss: Down from an upright position, or so that the other side faces up.
examples: The glass tipped *over*.
Turn the pancake *over* when it bubbles.
He rolled *over* and went back to sleep.

senses.gloss: Again, from the beginning.
examples: I made a mistake, so I had to start *over*.
Can I do the test *over*?
She said the same thing *over* and *over*.

senses.gloss: Remaining, not used.
examples: There's plenty of food left *over*.
Ten divided by three is three, with one left *over*.

senses.gloss: More than a stated amount, age, or time.
examples: The discount is for people 65 and *over*.
The meeting ran twenty minutes *over*.

senses.gloss: Carefully, from beginning to end.
examples: Think it *over* and let me know.
Look the contract *over* before you sign.

senses.gloss: To another person, side, or system.
examples: Hand *over* the keys.
We switched *over* to a new phone plan.

senses.gloss: Everywhere (in *all over*).
examples: I've looked all *over* for my glasses.
Students came from all *over* to study there.

position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but after a pronoun (*think it through*)
contrast: American *Monday through Friday* is a preposition meaning ‘up to and including’ (по пятницу включительно); British says *to*. *I'm through* (American) is an adjective meaning ‘I'm finished’. Spelling trap: *through* θruː, *though* ðoʊ, *thorough* ˈθɜːroʊ; *thru* is informal American. For через over a surface, use *across*.

senses.gloss: In at one side or end and out at the other.
examples: The gate was open, so we walked right *through*.
Move over and let the ambulance *through*.
Is the road still closed, or can we get *through*?

senses.gloss: From the beginning to the end.
senses.ru: до конца, от начала до конца
examples: Read the contract *through* before you sign.
You didn't think this *through*.
The baby slept *through* until six.

senses.gloss: Successfully past a test, stage, or obstacle.
examples: The deal finally went *through*.
Only four teams made it *through* to the finals.

senses.gloss: Connected by telephone.
examples: I tried calling, but I couldn't get *through*.
Hold on, I'll put you *through*.

senses.gloss: All the way to the final destination, without changing.
examples: This bus goes *through* to Boston.
Your bags are checked *through* to Denver.

position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but after a pronoun (*turn it off*)
contrast: *off* ɔːf and *of* əv are different words. American speech often says *off of* (*get off of the couch*), but careful writing uses *off* alone. *turn off* = выключить, *turn down* = убавить or отказать. *I'm off* means ‘I'm leaving’; *off* meaning ‘not fresh’ or ‘wrong’ (*The milk is off*) is an adjective.

senses.gloss: Away from a place; leaving.
examples: She waved and drove *off*.
The thief ran *off* with my bag.
I'm *off* to work; see you tonight.

senses.gloss: So as to be removed or no longer attached.
examples: Take your shoes *off* at the door.
A button came *off* my coat.
Wipe the dust *off* before you paint.

senses.gloss: So as to stop working or be disconnected.
examples: Turn *off* the lights when you leave.
Please switch your phones *off*.

senses.gloss: Away from work or duty.
examples: I'm taking Friday *off*.
She has two weeks *off* in August.

senses.gloss: As a reduction in price.
examples: Everything in the store is 30 percent *off*.
They took fifty dollars *off* because of the scratch.

senses.gloss: At a distance in space or time.
examples: Summer is still months *off*.
An island lay a few miles *off*.

senses.gloss: Completely, to the end.
examples: Let's finish *off* the pizza.
We finally paid *off* the car.

senses.gloss: So as to be canceled or ended.
examples: The game was called *off* because of rain.
They broke *off* the engagement.

senses.gloss: So as to be separated or closed to others.
examples: Police blocked *off* the street after the accident.
They fenced *off* the pool so the kids can't get in.

senses.gloss: Into sudden noise or explosion.
examples: My alarm went *off* at six.
Someone set *off* the fire alarm.

type: direction; also time (*from now on*) and particle
position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but after a pronoun (*put it on*)
contrast: *put on* is the action (надеть); *wear* or *have on* is the state (быть в чём-то): *She put on a coat*, *She had a coat on*. *from now on* needs the *on*: never *from now I'll…*. *What's on tonight?* and *The game is still on* are adjective uses. With an object *on* is a preposition: *on the table*.

senses.gloss: So as to work or be operating.
examples: Turn the lights *on*, please.
Did you leave the stove *on*?

senses.gloss: On the body, as clothing.
examples: Put your jacket *on*; it's cold.
She had a blue dress *on*.
Can I try these jeans *on*?

senses.gloss: Continuing, without stopping.
examples: Keep *on* trying.
Go *on*, I'm listening.
He talked *on* and *on* about his car.

senses.gloss: Forward from a point in time.
examples: From now *on*, please call before you come.
Later *on*, we'll talk about the budget.

senses.gloss: Onto or into a bus, train, plane, or ship.
examples: The bus stopped and we got *on*.
Hop *on*, I'll give you a ride.

senses.gloss: Attached, covering, or in position.
examples: Screw the lid *on* tight.
Is the cap still *on*?

senses.gloss: To the next person.
examples: Please pass the message *on*.
When you're done reading it, pass it *on* to Mike.

type: direction; also place and particle (*stop by*, *stand by*)
position: end — after the verb
contrast: *by* is far more often a preposition (*by bus*, *by Friday*, *written by*); the adverb has no object after it. *stop by* and *come by* mean a short visit, not ‘stop nearby’. *stand by* can mean ‘wait, ready’ (*Please stand by*) or ‘watch without acting’. Homophones: *buy*, *bye*.

senses.gloss: Past, going beyond someone or something.
examples: A truck roared *by*.
Days went *by* and still no news.
Excuse me, can I get *by*?

senses.gloss: To someone's home or office, for a short visit.
examples: Stop *by* my office after lunch.
Come *by* anytime.

senses.gloss: Managing to live or cope with what one has (in *get by*).
examples: We get *by* on one income.
My Spanish is good enough to get *by*.
How does anyone get *by* on minimum wage?

senses.gloss: Near, close at hand.
examples: Is there a gas station close *by*?
She stood *by*, watching.

senses.gloss: Ready and waiting (in *stand by*).
examples: Please stand *by* for further instructions.
Rescue crews are standing *by*.

position: end — after a verb of motion or of time passing
modifies: verbs of motion and of time passing
contrast: Spelling trap: *passed* is the past tense of *pass* (*A car passed us*); *past* is the adverb or preposition (*A car went past*). Both sound the same. *half past two* and *past the bank* are prepositions.

senses.gloss: Going by and beyond a person or place without stopping.
examples: A bus went *past* without stopping.
He walked right *past* and didn't say hi.
Summer flew *past*, and the kids were back in school.

position: end — after the verb or at the end of a set phrase
form: the short form of *around*, kept in a few set phrases
contrast: In American English *around* is the normal adverb: *turn around*, *go around*, *come around*, *the other way around*. *round* survives in *round and round* and *all year round* (also *year-round*); *the other way round* is still met in American reading but sounds British. British *come round for dinner* is American *come over*.

senses.gloss: In a circle, turning again and again (in *round and round*).
examples: The kids spun *round* and *round* on the carousel.
My thoughts kept going *round* and *round*.

senses.gloss: Through the whole year (in *all year round*).
examples: The pool is open all year *round*.
We grow herbs on the windowsill all year *round*.

senses.gloss: In the reverse way (in *the other way round*).
examples: It wasn't his fault; it was the other way *round*.
I thought she hired him, but it was the other way *round*.

position: end — after a verb of motion, or after *from* + a time
modifies: verbs of motion; time phrases after *from*
contrast: American *onward*, British *onwards*. *from 2010 on* and *from 2010 onward* mean the same; don't stack them. *Onward and upward!* is a set cheer meaning ‘keep going and improving’.

senses.gloss: Forward, farther along a route.
examples: The hikers pushed *onward* through the snow.
After lunch we drove *onward* to Denver.

senses.gloss: Forward in time from a stated point.
examples: From the 1990s *onward*, the city grew fast.
The museum is open from 9 a.m. *onward*.

position: end — after the verb
contrast: As an adverb the stress falls on *hill*; as an adjective before a noun it moves forward, and the adjective is also the figurative one: *an uphill battle* (тяжёлая борьба).

senses.gloss: Up a slope, toward the top of a hill.
examples: We pushed our bikes *uphill*.
The trail climbs *uphill* for two miles.
Water doesn't flow *uphill*.

position: end — after the verb
contrast: *It's all downhill from here* is an adjective use after *be*, and it can mean ‘it gets easier now’ or ‘it only gets worse now’ — context decides. *go downhill* on its own always means ‘get worse’. As an adjective before a noun the stress moves forward: *downhill skiing*.

senses.gloss: Down a slope.
examples: The kids raced *downhill* on their sleds.
The road runs *downhill* to the lake.

senses.gloss: Into a worse condition.
examples: After he lost his job, things went *downhill* fast.
The restaurant has gone *downhill* since the new owners took over.

position: end — after the verb
contrast: In American business and software writing *upstream* means ‘at an earlier stage’ or ‘at the source a project comes from’, and *downstream* ‘at a later stage’; the river picture is usually gone.

senses.gloss: Against the current, toward the source of a river.
examples: Salmon swim *upstream* to spawn.
We paddled *upstream* for an hour.

senses.gloss: At or toward an earlier stage of a process or supply chain.
examples: It's cheaper to fix the problem *upstream*, before the parts reach the factory.
Most of these errors start further *upstream*.

position: end — after the verb
contrast: In American business and software writing *downstream* means ‘at a later stage’ or ‘affected by an earlier step’, the opposite of *upstream*; the river picture is usually gone.

senses.gloss: With the current, away from the source of a river.
examples: The canoe drifted *downstream*.
The town is ten miles *downstream*.

senses.gloss: At or toward a later stage of a process.
examples: A mistake in the design causes bigger problems *downstream*.
Delays here ripple *downstream* to every other team.

position: end — after *go* or *lead someone*
contrast: Used almost only in *go astray* and *lead someone astray*. *stray* alone is a verb or adjective (*a stray dog*), not the adverb.

senses.gloss: Away from the right path or place, so as to get lost.
examples: My package went *astray* in the mail.
The hikers went *astray* in the fog.

senses.gloss: Into wrong behavior or a wrong belief.
senses.ru: сбить с пути (истинного); ввести в заблуждение
examples: Some older boys led him *astray*.
Don't let a single study lead you *astray*.

position: end — after *run* or *go*
contrast: Only about ships: *run aground*, *go aground* = сесть на мель. It does not mean *on the ground* (на земле).

senses.gloss: Onto the shore or the bottom of shallow water, so that a ship cannot move.
examples: The tanker ran *aground* off the coast of Alaska.
A cargo ship went *aground* in the fog.
The storm drove three fishing boats *aground*.

position: end — after the verb
contrast: *go overboard* is everyday informal English for doing too much (перебарщивать), and is far more common than the literal sense.

senses.gloss: To excess, further than is sensible (in *go overboard*).
examples: Don't go *overboard* with the decorations.
I went a little *overboard* on snacks for the party.

senses.gloss: Over the side of a boat or ship into the water.
examples: He fell *overboard* and had to be rescued.
Man *overboard*!

senses.gloss: Aside, so as to be abandoned (in *throw overboard*).
examples: The plan was thrown *overboard* when the budget was cut.
They tossed their principles *overboard* to win.
